06.01.title: Stress
06.01.html:
Statics told you the forces in a bike frame tube or a rail. It didn’t tell you whether the tube survives. A 2 kN force is nothing for a thick steel bar and fatal for a thin wire. What matters is how the force is spread over the material, and that is stress. This lesson defines it properly, as the thing that gives the force per area on any cut through a body.

Force per area on a cut

Cut a loaded body with a plane through a point, with unit normal n. The material on one side pushes and pulls on the other. Over a tiny area ΔA it exerts a force ΔF. The traction vector is

t(n)=ΔA→0lim​ΔAΔF​[N/m2=Pa; engineers use MPa=N/mm2].

Its component along n is the normal stress σn​=t⋅n (tension positive). The part in the plane is the shear stress τ. The traction depends on the plane you choose: the same point can carry pure tension on one plane and mostly shear on another.

The stress tensor

Cauchy’s result: you don’t need to know t on every plane. Nine numbers, the tractions on the three coordinate planes, give all the others:

t=σn,σ=​σxx​τxy​τxz​​τxy​σyy​τyz​​τxz​τyz​σzz​​​.

The proof is equilibrium of a tiny tetrahedron with three faces on the coordinate planes and one with normal n. Moment equilibrium of a tiny cube makes σ symmetric, so only six numbers are independent. Column j of σ is the traction on the plane with normal ej​.

Worked exampleA 3D stress state in a frame lug

σ=​80300​30−200​0010​​ MPa, plane normal n=(1,1,1)/3​.

  1. t=σn=(110,10,10)/3​=(63.51,5.77,5.77) MPa.
  2. Normal stress σn​=t⋅n=130/3=43.33 MPa.
  3. Shear τ=∣t∣2−σn2​​=47.14 MPa. On this plane the shear is larger than the tension.
  4. In 2D, a tube with 60 MPa axial and 25 MPa shear: the plane at 30° carries 66.65 MPa normal stress. Scanning every angle, the largest normal stress is 69.05 MPa, exactly the largest eigenvalue of σ (more in 06.07).

Exercise 1A tie rod

A steel tie rod of 16 mm diameter carries 30 kN. Find the axial stress, then the normal and shear stress on a plane cut at 45° to the axis.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. A=π⋅82=201.1 mm², so σ=30000/201.1=149.2 MPa.
  2. In the rod, σ=diag(149.2,0). With n=(cos45°,sin45°): t=(105.5,0) MPa.
  3. σn​=105.5⋅0.7071=74.6 MPa and τ=74.6 MPa: half the axial stress each. Ductile metals in tension fail by slip on such planes, which is why their fractures show 45° shear lips.

06.02.title: Strain
06.02.html:
Stress is what the material feels; strain is what you can measure. A strain gauge glued to a bridge girder or a bike crank reads how much the material stretches and distorts, and from that, via Hooke’s law, engineers infer the stress. This lesson defines strain from the displacement field and shows its one subtle point: rotations must not count as strain.

Displacement and its gradient

Every material point moves by a displacement u(x). A uniform u is a rigid translation: no deformation. What matters is how u changes from point to point, the displacement gradient ∇u with entries ∂ui​/∂xj​. Split it into a symmetric and an antisymmetric part:

∇u=ε (strain)21​(∇u+∇uT)​​+ω (rotation)21​(∇u−∇uT)​​.
  • εxx​=∂ux​/∂x is the stretch of a fibre along x (0.001 = 0.1 % = 1000 microstrain).
  • εxy​=21​(∂ux​/∂y+∂uy​/∂x) is half the change of a right angle. Engineers often use γxy​=2εxy​.
  • ω is a small rigid rotation and causes no stress.

Small strain and its limit

This small-strain tensor is linear in u, which makes everything downstream (beams, finite elements) linear. The price: a rigid rotation by θ shows up as a false strain of about −θ2/2. For rotations of a degree or less, that’s negligible. For a fishing rod or a rubber seal, you need large-deformation measures (such as the Green–Lagrange strain, which is exactly zero for any rigid rotation).

Worked exampleStrains from a displacement field

The code samples displacement fields on a 101 × 101 grid and differentiates them numerically.

  1. ux​=0.002x+0.0005y, uy​=0.0005x−0.0006y: εxx​=0.002, εyy​=−0.0006, εxy​=21​(0.0005+0.0005)=0.0005, rotation zero.
  2. A rigid rotation by 0.01 rad gives ∣εxx​∣=1−cos0.01=5.0×10−5, matching θ2/2. At 0.001 rad it falls 100 times, to 5×10−7: second order.
  3. A bending-like field ux​=−kxy, uy​=kx2/2 gives εxx​=−ky, varying linearly through the depth, with zero shear strain. That’s the beam theory of 06.09 in miniature.

Exercise 1A strain gauge rosette

Three gauges on a bike crank read ε0​=600×10−6 along x, ε90​=−180×10−6 along y, and ε45​=410×10−6 at 45°. Find γxy​. (The strain along a direction at angle φ is εxx​cos2φ+εyy​sin2φ+γxy​sinφcosφ.)

Show step-by-step solution
  1. At 45°: ε45​=21​(εxx​+εyy​)+21​γxy​.
  2. 410=21​(600−180)+21​γxy​=210+21​γxy​, so γxy​=400×10−6.
  3. That’s how every 45° rosette on a test rig works: three readings give the full 2D strain state.

quiz.q: εxy​ for ux​=0.002x+0.0005y, uy​=0.0005x−0.0006y.
quiz.explain: Half the sum of the cross derivatives.

quiz.q: False small strain from a rigid rotation of 0.02 rad (magnitude, θ2/2).
quiz.explain: Second order in θ.

quiz.q: γxy​ (microstrain) from the rosette exercise.
quiz.explain: ε45​=(εxx​+εyy​)/2+γxy​/2.

quiz.q: The antisymmetric part of ∇u describes…
quiz.explain: It causes no stress.

quiz.q: A 2 m bar stretches by 1.2 mm. Strain in microstrain.
quiz.explain: ΔL/L.

06.03.title: Hooke's law
06.03.html:
Stress and strain are linked by the material. For most engineering metals at working loads, and for bamboo along its fibres, the link is linear and reversible: double the load, double the stretch, unload and it springs back. That is Hooke’s law, and two numbers capture it for an isotropic material. This lesson builds the full 3D version as a 6 × 6 matrix and runs a virtual tensile test on it.

One dimension

Pull a bar: the axial strain is proportional to the stress, σ=Eε, with Young’s modulus E. The bar also gets thinner. The ratio of lateral contraction to axial stretch is Poisson’s ratio ν:

εlat​=−νεax​.

Typical values: steel E=210 GPa, ν=0.30; aluminium 70 GPa, 0.33; bamboo along the culm around 18 GPa (but far softer across it). For isotropic materials, ν lies between −1 and 0.5; rubber is close to 0.5 (nearly incompressible).

Three dimensions

Superpose the three directions and add shear, τ=Gγ:

εxx​=E1​[σxx​−ν(σyy​+σzz​)],γxy​=Gτxy​​,G=2(1+ν)E​.

Inverted, with the Lamé constants λ=(1+ν)(1−2ν)Eν​ and μ=G:

σ=λtr(ε)I+2με.

In Voigt notation the six stresses and six strains (with engineering shear strains) become vectors and the law becomes σ=Cε with a 6 × 6 matrix. Finite element programs store exactly that. The bulk modulus K=E/(3(1−2ν)) links pressure to volume change: ΔV/V=−p/K.

Worked exampleA virtual tensile test

The code builds C from E and ν, applies σxx​=100 MPa alone, and solves for the strains.

  1. Steel: λ=121.15 GPa, G=80.77 GPa, K=175 GPa. The test returns E=210 GPa and ν=0.3 exactly, with εyy​=εzz​ and no shear strain.
  2. Aluminium: G=26.32 GPa, K=68.63 GPa.
  3. 100 MPa hydrostatic pressure on steel: volume strain −100/175000=−5.71×10−4.
  4. A 300 mm steel bar of 20 mm diameter at 100 MPa gets 0.143 mm longer and 2.86 µm thinner.

Exercise 1A rubber pad and a steel block

A cube is squeezed with 10 MPa on the top face while its sides are free. Compare the lateral expansion of steel (E=210 GPa, ν=0.3) and of rubber (E=5 MPa, ν=0.49), as strains.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Steel: εax​=−10/210000=−4.76×10−5, lateral +0.3⋅4.76×10−5=1.43×10−5.
  2. Rubber: εax​=−10/5=−2. That’s far beyond small strain, so the linear law no longer applies, which is the real lesson. At 0.1 MPa instead, εax​=−0.02 and lateral +0.0098: the rubber bulges almost as much as it shortens, keeping its volume.

quiz.q: Shear modulus G (GPa) of steel, E=210 GPa, ν=0.3. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: E/(2(1+ν)).

quiz.q: Bulk modulus K (GPa) of steel.
quiz.explain: E/(3(1−2ν)).

quiz.q: Strain (microstrain) of aluminium at 140 MPa, E=70 GPa.
quiz.explain: σ/E.

quiz.q: Lamé constant λ (GPa) for steel. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: Eν/((1+ν)(1−2ν)).

quiz.q: A material with ν close to 0.5 is…
quiz.explain: K→∞ as ν→0.5.

06.04.title: Axial bars
06.04.html:
Rods, cables, bolts, truss members and brake cables mostly carry axial force. How much they stretch matters: a brake lever that travels too far feels spongy, a bolt that stretches loses clamping force, and a lift cable that stretches lets the cabin bounce. For a bar the answer is one formula, and this lesson extends it to stepped and tapered bars and to self-weight.

The bar formula

A bar of length L, area A and modulus E carrying an axial force N has stress σ=N/A and strain ε=σ/E. Uniform strain means the elongation is

δ=εL=EANL​.

EA is the axial stiffness of the section and EA/L the spring stiffness of the bar. When N, A or E change along the bar, add up the pieces, or integrate:

δ=i∑​Ei​Ai​Ni​Li​​,δ=∫0L​EA(x)N(x)​dx.

Find each segment’s internal force Ni​ by a cut and an FBD (lesson 05.06), then add the stretches.

Self-weight and tapers

A cable of density ρ hanging under its own weight carries N(x)=ρgA(L−x), so δ=ρgL2/(2E), independent of the area. A round bar tapering linearly from radius r1​ to r2​ gives δ=PL/(Eπr1​r2​).

Worked exampleA brake cable and a stepped bar

  1. The brake cable from lesson 05.12: steel, 1.5 mm diameter, 1.8 m, 168 N. A=1.767 mm², σ=95.1 MPa, δ=168⋅1800/(200000⋅1.767)=0.856 mm. (Stranded cable is softer than solid wire, so the real figure is larger.)
  2. Stepped bar fixed at a wall: steel 400 mm × Ø20 next to the wall, aluminium 300 mm × Ø30 beyond it. 30 kN pulls at the free end, 10 kN pushes back at the joint. Cuts give N=20 kN in the steel and 30 kN in the aluminium.
  3. δ=20000⋅400/(210000⋅314.2)+30000⋅300/(70000⋅706.9)=0.1213+0.1819=0.3032 mm.
  4. A 1 km steel cable hanging free stretches 7850⋅9.81⋅10002/(2⋅210×109)=0.183 m under its own weight.

Exercise 1A lift rod

A 6 m steel hanger rod of 24 mm diameter carries a 45 kN floor load at its lower end. Find the stress and the stretch. What diameter keeps the stretch under 2 mm?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. A=π⋅122=452.4 mm², σ=45000/452.4=99.5 MPa.
  2. δ=45000⋅6000/(210000⋅452.4)=2.84 mm.
  3. For δ≤2 mm: A≥45000⋅6000/(210000⋅2)=642.9 mm², so d≥28.6 mm. Use 30 mm.

quiz.q: Stretch (mm) of the 1.8 m brake cable at 168 N. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: NL/(EA).

quiz.q: Total stretch (mm) of the stepped bar. 4 decimals.
quiz.explain: Sum of the two segments.

quiz.q: Stretch (mm) of the 6 m lift rod, 24 mm diameter, 45 kN. 3 decimals.
quiz.explain: NL/(EA).

quiz.q: Self-weight stretch (mm) of a 500 m steel cable (ρ=7850, E=210 GPa). 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: ρgL2/(2E).

quiz.q: Doubling a bar’s diameter changes its stretch under the same load by a factor of…
quiz.explain: The area grows fourfold.

06.05.title: Statically indeterminate bars
06.05.html:
Lesson 05.08 flagged structures where statics alone can’t find the forces. Now you have the missing ingredient: deformation. A bar clamped between two walls, a steel bolt inside an aluminium sleeve, a concrete column with steel bars inside it. All are solved with the same three-step recipe, and the answers say something important: stiffness attracts load.

The three ingredients

  1. Equilibrium: the force equations you’d write anyway. They have more unknowns than equations.
  2. Compatibility: a geometric condition on the deformations. For a bar between rigid walls, the total stretch must be zero. For parts bolted together, they must stretch by the same amount.
  3. Constitutive law: Hooke’s law, δ=NL/(EA), links forces to deformations.

Put the force–deformation law into the compatibility condition and you get the extra equations you need.

A bar between two walls

A bar between rigid walls carries a load P at the point where part 1 (length a, stiffness E1​A1​, at wall A) meets part 2 (length b, stiffness E2​A2​, at wall B). Part 1 is in tension RA​ and part 2 in compression RB​.

RA​+RB​=P,E1​A1​RA​a​=E2​A2​RB​b​.

For a uniform bar, RA​=Pb/L and RB​=Pa/L: the wall closer to the load takes more. In general each part takes load in proportion to its spring stiffness EA/L. That is the principle behind every indeterminate structure: load goes where the stiffness is.

Stiffness matrices

The same answer comes from treating each part as a spring with stiffness k=EA/L, assembling a stiffness matrix and solving Ku=f for the free nodal displacements. That is the 1D finite element method, which the code uses as a cross-check, and it scales to any number of parts and loads.

Worked exampleTwo walls, two materials

  1. Uniform steel bar, L=1000 mm, 60 kN at a=300 mm: RA​=60⋅700/1000=42 kN, RB​=18 kN. The load point moves 42000⋅300/(210000⋅400)=0.15 mm.
  2. Steel 300 mm (A=400 mm²) next to wall A and aluminium 700 mm (A=600 mm²) next to wall B. Flexibilities a/(E1​A1​)=3.571×10−6 and b/(E2​A2​)=1.667×10−5 mm/N.
  3. RA​=60⋅16.667/(3.571+16.667)=49.41 kN and RB​=10.59 kN. The short steel part carries 123.5 MPa, the long aluminium part only 17.6 MPa.
  4. With 25 kN and 8 kN at two points on a three-part bar, the stiffness model gives reactions 24.23 and 8.77 kN, summing to the 33 kN applied.

Exercise 1A bolt and a sleeve

A steel bolt (A=80 mm²) passes through an aluminium sleeve (A=240 mm²) of the same length. A 30 kN compressive load is applied to both through rigid end plates. How is the load shared?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Equilibrium: Ns​+Na​=30 kN.
  2. Compatibility: same length, same shortening, so Ns​/(Es​As​)=Na​/(Ea​Aa​).
  3. Stiffnesses: Es​As​=210000⋅80=16.8 MN and Ea​Aa​=70000⋅240=16.8 MN. Equal, so each carries 15 kN. Stresses: 187.5 MPa in the bolt and 62.5 MPa in the sleeve. Equal force, very different stress.

quiz.q: Wall A reaction (kN) for 60 kN at 300 mm on a uniform 1 m bar.
quiz.explain: Pb/L.

quiz.q: Wall A reaction (kN) in the steel/aluminium bar. 2 decimals.
quiz.explain: Load in proportion to stiffness.

quiz.q: Stress (MPa) in the bolt of the bolt-and-sleeve exercise. 1 decimal.
quiz.explain: Half the load on 80 mm².

quiz.q: In an indeterminate structure, load goes preferentially to…
quiz.explain: Compatibility shares load by stiffness.
